message.content:
This hybrid simulator is built with QEMU and verilator. 
To support running of linux kernel application and MMIO, we have to exchange many architecture states.
I have an idea, we could develop a dynamic binary translator for the RISC-V ISA within the verilator, so we don't have to do IPC between QEMU and verilator. What do you think? consider how Imperas’ ImperasDV work?

content.text:
My take: the direction (functional model in the same process as the RTL) is a proven pattern, but I would not build a DBT from scratch, and being in-process does not remove the hard part of Linux support - it only removes the transport, which is already the cheap part.

**What ImperasDV actually is.** It is a lockstep *verification* tool, not a fast-forward tool. The Imperas reference model (an ISS) is linked into the simulator process as a library. Every time the RTL retires an instruction, the testbench reports it over RVVI (RISC-V Verification Interface), the reference model steps one instruction, and the two architectural states are compared. Async events (interrupts) are forwarded as net changes. Note: it does not avoid state exchange - it exchanges state on *every retired instruction*. Being in-process is what makes that bandwidth affordable. Its use case matches your `--cosim` lockstep work, not the QEMU1 -> vsim handoff.

**What in-process would buy us - and what it would not:**

- Our handoff IPC is one file write plus a shared mmap, a few ms, once per ROI. Killing it saves almost nothing.
- ResumeDriver/StateDrain stay either way. State still has to enter the RTL hart through the Debug Module; that code does not care where the functional model lives.
- The real Linux blockers are device and interrupt state: CLINT mtime/mtimecmp, PLIC pending/enable, UART FIFOs, in-flight IRQs. That mapping problem is identical in-process or cross-process.
- The CPU side is closer than it looks: satp plus the page tables already live in the shared mmap, and the TLB is transparent (cold TLB after handoff is a warmup error, not a correctness bug). So Linux CPU state is mostly "add S-mode CSRs to `hybrid_state_v1`".

**If we did want in-process, never write our own DBT.** A Linux-grade RV64GCV translator is a multi-year project, and QEMU already is one. The realistic options, in order of fit:

1. **Dromajo** (Esperanto) - a RISC-V emulator built exactly for this: embedded in RTL cosim, checkpoint/restore, boots Linux. Closest match to your idea.
2. **Spike** - the standard DV reference model; Chipyard's SpikeTile embeds it inside the simulated SoC sharing the memory system.
3. **QEMU as a library** (QBox/libqemu style) - keeps TCG speed but QEMU is not designed as a library; heaviest integration.

Trade-off: Dromajo/Spike are interpreters, roughly 5-20x slower than QEMU's TCG. For Linux workloads the fast-forward leg is billions of instructions, so losing TCG speed can dominate total wall time.

**My recommendation:** keep QEMU for fast-forward and attack Linux support inside the current architecture - extend `hybrid_state_v1` with S-mode CSRs, define quiescent-point handoff rules (no pending IRQs, drained FIFOs, copy mtime/mtimecmp), and lean on the shared mmap for page tables. Consider an embedded ISS (Dromajo) only if lockstep DV becomes a first-class goal, because that is where in-process genuinely wins - it would make `--cosim` much faster than the current replay-from-boot oracle.

One question that decides the direction: is the driver for this Linux *performance estimation*, or *lockstep verification* of the RTL? If the latter, the ImperasDV-style embedded reference is the right architecture and worth a roadmap entry.

aiTitle: Develop RISC-V dynamic binary translator for verilator

content.text:
Short version: embedding an existing ISS is 1-2 person-months; wrapping QEMU as an in-process library is 3-6 months plus permanent fork maintenance; writing your own DBT is 2-3 person-years before it boots Linux reliably - and the validation tail, not the translator, is where the years go.

**Option by option:**

**1. Write our own DBT (the literal idea) - 2-3+ person-years.**

| Piece | Effort | Why |
|---|---|---|
| RV64GC interpreter core | 2-3 months | well-trodden, references exist |
| JIT: translation cache, block chaining, softmmu, precise traps | 8-12 months | this is the actual "DBT" part; QEMU took years here |
| RVV 1.0 | 3-6 months | ~600 instruction variants x LMUL/SEW/masking/tail rules; ax45mpv is a vector CPU, so not optional |
| Devices for Linux boot (CLINT, PLIC, UART, virtio) | 2-3 months | straightforward but real |
| Andes custom CSRs/extensions | unknown | your QEMU fork already carries these; a new DBT starts from zero |
| Validation | the long tail | riscv-arch-test, riscof, Linux boot debug; a wrong-translation bug surfaces as a kernel panic millions of instructions later |

The translator is maybe 30% of the work. Debugging silent wrong-execution is the other 70%, and it never fully ends: every new extension (Zb*, Zc*, vector crypto, future Andes ISA) becomes your job forever. QEMU gives you that maintenance for free today.

**2. QEMU as an in-process library (QBox style) - 3-6 person-months + ongoing.** Not crazy: vsim is SystemC and QBox is exactly QEMU-in-SystemC/TLM. The hard parts are time synchronization (TCG runs in free quanta, Verilator runs clocked - keeping them coherent is fiddly) and rebasing the QBox patch set onto the Andes QEMU fork, then carrying it across every QEMU upgrade.

**3. Embed Spike - 1-2 person-months.** It is already a C++ library; `state_t` exposes GPRs/FPRs/vector regs/CSRs directly, it has CLINT/PLIC/UART, boots Linux, and has full RVV. The integration work is wiring its memory to the shared mmap and calling ResumeDriver at the switch point. Cost: roughly 10-50x slower than TCG, which hurts when the fast-forward leg is billions of instructions.

**4. Embed Dromajo - 1-2 person-months,** purpose-built for RTL cosim checkpointing. But as far as I know it is RV64GC only, no RVV - I have not verified this recently, but if true it is disqualifying for a vector CPU. Worth checking before it enters any plan.

**The comparison that matters:** extending the current architecture for Linux (S-mode CSRs in `hybrid_state_v1`, quiescent-point handoff rules, mtime/mtimecmp sync) is roughly 1-2 person-months. So the homegrown DBT costs 15-25x more than the incremental path, and when it is done, the device-state and interrupt problems - the actual Linux blockers - are still sitting there unchanged, because they live at the functional-to-RTL boundary, not in the IPC.

If the long-term goal turns out to be lockstep DV, option 3 (Spike in-process) is the cheapest way to get the ImperasDV-style architecture without betting years on a new translator.
